decision: How should the child's test screen be built: where do the question, the answer input, the whiteboard and the progress sit, and how does the child move through the test?
primary_axis: screen model for taking the test (layout of question, answer, whiteboard and progress, plus the navigation model)
where: Live prototype at /test-prototype?variant=A..E (src/app/test-prototype, src/components/test-prototype). Branch site/assessment-test-prototype; not for merge. The route 404s in production builds. Run: PORT=3060 npm run dev. The dark bar at the bottom switches variants (arrows or keyboard left/right) and jumps to Q1, Q4 (a show-your-work question), Q18, Break, Facts, Q19, Q36 and End.
invariants: same fake grade 3 test for a child named Maya: 36 questions from 8 templates, 7 of them need shown work (D-083 count for grades 3-5)
same order: questions 1-18, halfway break (skippable), 60-second facts section (addition and subtraction to 20, what BC expects in grade 3), questions 19-36, end screen
same rules: an answer is needed, and on a show-your-work question the whiteboard must have work; the whiteboard draws with mouse, finger or stylus and has a Type tab
same 'read it to me' (browser speech; hidden when the browser has none), same on-screen number pad that also takes the keyboard
same end message: the report will be emailed to the grown-up shortly
same tokens: Geist, warm look colours, 6 px controls; every tap target 44 px or more
all five fit 1440x900, 1024x768 and 768x1024 with no page scroll (checked with a script on all 75 screens)
events through the track helper: test_start, test_break (shown, rested, skipped), test_facts_done, test_finish, read_aloud, each with src = proto-<variant>
count_note: Five options because Savar asked for 5 (D-086), above the usual 2-4.

options.name: Workbook page
options.bet: Each question is one page of a paper workbook: question, answer boxes and a squared working space on the same page; progress is 'Page 5 of 36'; the facts section is a drill sheet
options.benefit: Matches the brand (paper workbooks) and the books the child gets next; the working space is always in view, so showing work feels normal
options.cost: Less room for big answer targets; the page is busy for a grade 1 child
options.risk: 'Page 5 of 36' may feel long; a paper look on a screen can feel fake

options.name: Split desk
options.bet: Question and answer on the left, a full-height whiteboard on the right on every question; progress is 36 segments with a dot for the halfway break
options.benefit: The most room for shown work, so the best work images for the report and the AI review; good with a stylus
options.cost: Half the screen is a whiteboard even on questions that do not need it
options.risk: Children may scribble on the board all the time, and the empty board may distract

options.name: One big thing
options.bet: One huge question and four large coloured answer tiles, nothing else; the whiteboard is a full-screen sheet, and on a show-your-work question it opens as step 2 after the answer; 'read every question' option
options.benefit: Lowest load for ages 6-8; the largest touch targets; the read-aloud is the first thing on the screen
options.cost: Shown work is a separate step, so it takes longer on the 7 work questions
options.risk: Children skip optional work because the board is hidden; the AI gets fewer work images

options.name: Trail
options.bet: Progress is the main picture: a trail with 36 stops, a halfway camp (break and facts) and a finish flag; the question is a card; the whiteboard is a drawer that opens by itself on show-your-work questions
options.benefit: Most motivating over 30-45 minutes; the break and the facts section have a place in the story
options.cost: The trail takes height; the number pad becomes one row of keys to fit
options.risk: Reads as a game; 36 stops in view can make the test look long; less like the paper brand

options.name: School test
options.bet: The layout children know from school online tests (FSA, EQAO): a tool rail (read aloud, whiteboard, bigger text), a question map, Back and Next; the child can skip and come back within a part, and the end of a part lists what is not finished
options.benefit: Lets the child go back and skip (the research found this helps younger children); familiar from grade 4 on; the bigger-text tool
options.cost: Dense; the most chrome; the map of 18 squares is a lot for a grade 1 child
options.risk: Feels like an exam, which raises stress; going back interacts with the two-stage routing (allowed only inside a part here)

evidence.screenshots: shots/<option>-<screen>-<viewport>.png; screens q1, q4work, break, facts, end; viewports laptop 1440x900, tablet-land 1024x768, tablet-port 768x1024
checks: click-through of each option: answer, draw, next, facts start and enter, end (in-browser script)
stylus and touch strokes reach the whiteboard; C's work step needs a stroke before 'Done, next question' turns on
no page scroll and no tap target under 44 px on all 75 screens
npx eslint src (0 errors) and npm run build pass
not_checked: a real tablet or stylus (only emulated touch and pen events)
voice quality on Windows, Chromebook and iPad voices (the bar shows the voice the browser picked; on this Mac: Samantha, en-US)
children: no child has used any option yet
